questions.q: Per this lesson, what specifically does a successful `verify()` call from Lesson 22 prove, and what doesn't it cover?
options: It proves the user controlled that address at the moment they signed, but says nothing about subsequent requests — a session is needed to carry that forward
It proves the user will remain logged in forever, with no further session mechanism needed
It proves the user's wallet balance, not their identity
It proves nothing useful on its own and must always be paired with a JWT
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as the exact gap sessions fill: verification is a moment-in-time proof, and HTTP's statelessness means later requests need something else tying them back to it.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff this lesson identifies between a server-side session and a JWT?
options: A server-side session allows real-time revocation by deleting the stored record; a JWT scales without a shared store but can't be revoked before it expires
JWTs are always more secure than server-side sessions in every scenario
Server-side sessions cannot store a user's wallet address, only JWTs can
There is no real tradeoff; the lesson says they are functionally identical
questions.explain: The lesson states this tradeoff explicitly: server-side sessions can be revoked instantly by deleting the record, while a JWT remains valid until its expiry regardless of what the backend does.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what two triggers does a Web3 session have to handle beyond a normal web session's logout?
options: A wallet disconnecting, and a wallet switching accounts
A browser tab closing, and a page refresh
A smart contract being upgraded, and a gas price spike
An RPC provider going offline, and a block reorg
questions.explain: The lesson lists these two Web3-specific triggers explicitly, each requiring the frontend to actively invalidate the session rather than just update local UI state.

questions.q: What specific bug does this lesson describe if a frontend fails to invalidate a session when the wallet switches accounts?
options: Requests can appear to come from the new account's UI while still being authorized as the old, previously verified address
The application crashes immediately on any new request
The user is permanently logged out of all accounts
The session automatically re-verifies itself using the new address with no further action needed
questions.explain: The lesson calls this out as a real, exploitable bug: the UI shows the new account while the session quietly keeps authorizing the old, unchanged one.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a session needs an expiry even though a SIWE signature itself might not expire?
options: An expiry bounds how long a leaked session cookie or token stays useful to whoever obtained it
SIWE signatures are always invalid after 24 hours regardless of session settings
Session expiry is required by the EIP-4361 specification for every implementation
Without expiry, the siwe library's verify() function would refuse to run at all
questions.explain: The lesson makes this point directly: the session's own expiry limits the damage window if the session credential (cookie or token) ever leaks, independent of the signature's own validity.
